# Abstract

The century separating the Battle of Plassey in June 1757 from the outbreak of the Indian Rebellion in May 1857 witnessed the territorial conquest, fiscal consolidation and commercial restructuring of the South Asian subcontinent under the English East India Company. Encompassing 4,35M km² (4.353.693 km² across 56.456 active 5-arcminute terrestrial cells) spanning six administrative divisions, regional population expanded from 185M in 1757AD to 188M in 1775AD, 204M in 1800AD, 215M in 1820AD, 229M in 1840AD and 244M in 1857AD, representing an aggregate secular expansion of 31,9% at an average annual compound growth rate of 0,28%. This demographic growth occurred amidst severe ecological, institutional and economic dislocations, including catastrophic mortality famines, colonial revenue extractions, the dismantling of artisanal textile manufacturing and the spatial reorientation of urban hierarchies toward maritime export gateways.

Demographic mass remained heavily concentrated across the alluvial Gangetic basin and southern river deltas. Bengal Presidency accommodated 51,8M people in 1757AD (28% of subcontinent population; 6.444,12 persons per 100 km² across 803.833 km²), rising to 68,32M by 1857AD (8.499,28 persons per 100 km²), despite losing an estimated 10M inhabitants during the devastating famine of 1770AD. The North-Western Provinces and Oudh housed 35,15M inhabitants in 1757AD across 289.686 km², expanding to 46,36M in 1857AD and sustaining the highest demographic density on the subcontinent, which rose from 12.133,83 to 16.003,54 persons per 100 km². Madras Presidency, Mysore and Travancore supported 31,45M in 1757AD across 634.549 km², reaching 41,48M in 1857AD (6.536,93 persons per 100 km²). Bombay Presidency, the Maratha Deccan, Gujarat and Sindh grew from 24,05M across 633.638 km² to 31,72M (5.005,99 persons per 100 km²). The vast northern expanse of Punjab, Jammu-Kashmir, Rajputana and Central India accommodated 37M people in 1757AD across 1.744.582 km², expanding to 48,8M in 1857AD (2.797,23 persons per 100 km²). British Ceylon, Nepal, Bhutan and the Maldives protectorate supported 5,55M inhabitants in 1757AD across 247.405 km², rising to 7,32M in 1857AD (2.958,71 persons per 100 km²).

This historical demographic synthesis integrates 1.355 catalogued settlements with continuous longitudinal population trajectories, reconciled against 2.155 candidate records in the INDUS source ledger alongside 800 documented exclusions. By subtracting nucleated city populations from sub-regional demographic totals, rural populations are dasymetrically distributed across agricultural grid cells weighted by river proximity, soil productivity, canal headworks and precipitation gradients. The resulting analysis captures the dramatic divergence between growing colonial port metropolises—most notably Mumbai (which expanded from 100k to 659,6k inhabitants), Kolkata (reaching 390,3k) and Chennai (reaching 341,5k)—and declining interior manufacturing capitals such as Murshidabad, Dhaka and Patna, demonstrating how colonial fiscal policy and international trade transformed the economic geography of South Asia prior to direct Crown governance.

# Background

## Political Consolidation and Territorial Expansion

The century between 1757AD and 1857AD witnessed the piecemeal transformation of the English East India Company from a joint-stock trading enterprise operating out of fortified coastal factories into an imperial territorial sovereign commanding an army of over 200.000 men [@Torri2014Periodizat; @Verghese2019Conquest]. The military victory of Robert Clive at Plassey in June 1757, followed by the Battle of Buxar in 1764AD, secured the grant of the *diwani* (revenue administration) of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa from the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II in 1765AD [@NoguesMarco2021Measuring; @Bagchi2015Colonialis]. This fiscal concession transferred direct command over the agrarian surplus of South Asia's richest province to company officials, establishing the financial apparatus that funded subsequent military expansion across the subcontinent.

Subsequent territorial annexations proceeded through shifting diplomatic coalitions, military conquests and coercive subsidiary alliances [@Lawrence2024Political]. Under Governor-General Richard Wellesley (1798AD to 1805AD), the Company neutralised Tipu Sultan of Mysore in 1799AD, annexed coastal Karnataka and Thanjavur, partitioned the territories of the Nizam of Hyderabad and compelled the Nawab of Oudh to cede Rohilkhand and the lower Doab [@Verghese2019Conquest]. The second and third Anglo-Maratha wars (1803AD to 1805AD and 1817AD to 1818AD) crushed the Maratha Confederacy, transferring direct control over western India, Gujarat and the Peshwa's territories to the Bombay Presidency, while placing Rajput principalities under British paramountcy [@Gust2018Perilous; @Torri2014Periodizat]. In the northwest, the annexation of Sindh by Charles Napier in 1843AD and the defeat of the Sikh Empire in the Anglo-Sikh wars (1845AD to 1849AD) brought Punjab and the trans-Indus frontier under Company administration, concluding with James Broun-Ramsay, Marquess of Dalhousie's annexation of Oudh in 1856AD under the doctrine of lapse [@Peers1998Soldiers; @Lawrence2024Political].

## Agrarian Tenures and Revenue Extraction Systems

Colonial rule imposed novel property frameworks designed to extract agrarian revenues with administrative predictability and maximum fiscal yield [@Sarwar2012Comparativ; @Bagchi2015Colonialis]. In Bengal, Bihar and coastal Orissa, Lord Cornwallis enacted the Permanent Settlement of 1793AD, which transformed indigenous tax farmers and hereditary collectors (*zamindars*) into private landlords holding absolute proprietary titles, while fixing the state land revenue assessment in perpetuity at 26,8M rupees [@Sarwar2012Comparativ; @NoguesMarco2021Measuring]. While intended to foster improving landlords on the English model, the draconian sunset law—mandating the public auction of any estate whose revenue was not paid by sunset on the appointed date—resulted in the bankruptcy and transfer of nearly half the landed estates of Bengal within two decades, pauperising peasant cultivators (*raiyats*) who were reduced to rack-rented tenants-at-will [@Bagchi2015Colonialis; @LahiriDutt2014Commodifie].

In southern and western India, administrative dissatisfaction with the zamindari model led Thomas Munro and Mountstuart Elphinstone to institute the *ryotwari* system across Madras and Bombay Presidencies [@Sarwar2012Comparativ; @Roy2018State]. This system bypassed intermediary landlords, assessing revenue directly on individual peasant cultivators based on detailed cadastral soil surveys. However, revenue demand was fixed at onerous rates ranging from 45% to 55% of gross produce, payable strictly in cash, which compelled cultivators to borrow from village moneylenders and exposed them to dispossession during years of harvest failure [@Sarwar2012Comparativ; @Roy2007Globalisat]. Across the North-Western Provinces and Punjab, administrators developed the *mahalwari* system, assessing revenue jointly on village communities and coparcenary brotherhoods (*bhaiachara*), which preserved communal village institutions but imposed heavy collective tax burdens that intensified rural inequality and social friction [@Sarwar2012Comparativ; @Cassan2020Enfranchis].

## De-Industrialisation and Commercial Transition

Prior to the mid-eighteenth century, South Asia functioned as the foremost textile workshop of the world, exporting cotton calicoes, muslins and silks across the Indian Ocean basin and Europe [@Riello2009India]. Following Plassey, the East India Company deployed its monopolistic political authority to subjugate artisanal producers, forcing weavers into exclusive monopsonistic supply contracts at artificially depressed prices [@Riello2009India; @Clingingsmith2017Deindustri]. Between 1800AD and 1830AD, the technological breakthrough of steam-powered cotton spinning and weaving in Lancashire, paired with British import duties on Indian textiles exceeding 70%, reversed international trade flows [@Riello2009India; @Clingingsmith2017Deindustri; @Roy2007Globalisat].

British manufactured twist, yarn and piece goods inundated the subcontinent, dismantling artisanal cotton spinning and severely depressing urban handloom weaving [@Clingingsmith2017Deindustri; @Roy2022Review]. Renowned textile manufacturing metropolises suffered rapid economic and demographic contraction: Dhaka, celebrated for delicate muslins, saw its population decline from over 200k in 1757AD to 146,4k in 1800AD and fewer than 70k by the 1830s, while Murshidabad, the former nawabi capital, contracted from 180k to 146,4k [@Riello2009India; @Roy2014Geography]. Millions of displaced weavers, spinners and ancillary artisans were driven out of manufacturing into low-productivity subsistence agriculture, raising agrarian land-labour ratios and deepening rural vulnerability [@Bagchi2015Colonialis; @Roy2018Employment]. Simultaneously, the subcontinent was converted into an exporter of primary agricultural commodities—raw cotton, opium for the Canton trade, indigo, tea and raw silk—generating an unrequited drain of wealth that drained investable capital from the regional economy [@NoguesMarco2021Measuring; @Bagchi2015Colonialis].

## Subsistence Insecurity, Ecological Crises and Epidemics

The demographic trajectory of the subcontinent under Company rule was repeatedly interrupted by severe subsistence crises and epidemic mortality shocks [@Mallik2022Colonial; @Major2020British]. The Great Bengal Famine of 1770AD, triggered by monsoon failure in 1769AD but intensely aggravated by Company grain hoarding, coercive revenue collection and the refusal to remit land taxes, claimed an estimated 10M lives—approximately one-third of the population of Bengal and Bihar [@Mallik2022Colonial; @Eskander2024Famine]. In 1783AD, the Chalisa famine devastated northern India, depopulating large tracts of the North-Western Provinces, Rajasthan and Punjab [@Major2020British; @Mehta2021Politics]. Between 1791AD and 1792AD, the Doji bara or skull famine swept through the Deccan, Gujarat and Madras, producing extensive mortality and mass distress migrations [@Major2020British; @Bhattacharya2012Contagion].

Subsequent subsistence crises in 1803AD, 1812AD, 1824AD, 1833AD (the Guntur famine) and 1837AD to 1838AD (the Agra famine) demonstrated the persistence of severe vulnerability [@Major2020British; @Meena2016Railway]. Adherence to strict laissez-faire political economy prevented colonial officials from intervening to regulate grain prices or establish comprehensive relief works, while traditional village grain reserves had been eliminated by heavy cash taxation [@Major2020British; @Bagchi2015Colonialis]. Famine conditions systematically triggered explosive outbreaks of epidemic disease, including waterborne cholera, epidemic malaria and smallpox, which swept along troop movement corridors and commercial highways [@Bhattacharya2012Contagion; @Peers1998Soldiers; @George2023Trained]. These demographic crises curtailed net population growth, holding annual secular increases to modest rates across the entire century.

# Methodology

## Spatial Disaggregation and Territorial Masking

To reconstruct demographic patterns across 4.353.693 km² of land area, the INDUS spatial framework partitions the subcontinent into 56.456 active 5-arcminute raster cells (approximately 9,2 km by 9,2 km at tropical latitudes). Territorial boundaries conform to the documented limits of British direct rule and tributary princely states in 1857AD, excluding extraterritorial waters and unpopulated mountain glaciers.

Each terrestrial cell is evaluated against environmental, hydrological and infrastructural covariates:
- Fluvial proximity: distance decay functions calibrated to perennial rivers (the Ganges, Yamuna, Brahmaputra, Indus, Narmada, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri), with exponential population density attenuation beyond 12 km in dry tracts [@LahiriDutt2014Commodifie; @Roy2014Geography].
- Agro-ecological suitability: baseline soil moisture regimes, distinguishing fertile alluvial silts, deep black cotton soils (regur) of the Deccan, red laterites and arid sandy plains of the Thar desert [@Fujita2020Sustainabl; @Bava2017Sustainabl].
- Monsoon precipitation isohyets: interpolating historical precipitation surfaces, accounting for the steep drop from over 1.500 mm in Bengal and coastal Malabar to under 250 mm in Sindh and western Rajasthan [@Mehta2021Politics].
- Topographic constraints: slope penalties applied to rugged mountain zones across the Himalayas, Western Ghats, Vindhyas and Aravalis, weighting population into broad river basins, coastal plains and interfluvial plains [@Roy2014Geography].

## Settlement Integration and Dasymetric Allocation

To prevent double counting between nucleated urban inhabitants and rural cultivators, 1.355 catalogued settlements with continuous longitudinal demographic series are geocoded to WGS84 coordinates. At each benchmark year (1757AD, 1775AD, 1800AD, 1820AD, 1840AD and 1857AD), the population of active catalogued settlements within each of the six administrative divisions is summed and subtracted from the sub-regional demographic envelope.

The residual rural population is then dasymetrically distributed across non-settled terrestrial cells in proportion to cell suitability weights. A boundary feathering filter smoothes density transitions along administrative borders, preventing artificial step cliffs between adjacent collectorates or princely states [@Kapur2006British; @Roy2018State].

## Uncertainty Envelopes and Variance Calibration

Because decennial synchronous all-India censuses began only in 1871AD and 1881AD, demographic estimates for the pre-1857AD era rely upon district revenue surveys, hearth and house counts, collectorate returns and retrospective demographic modeling [@Roy2018State; @Cassan2020Enfranchis]. To capture archival uncertainty, each sub-regional benchmark estimate is bounded by explicit confidence intervals (+/- 14% to 15% across all divisions). For the 1857AD benchmark, the regional total of 244M inhabitants is bounded between 209,8M and 278,2M.

# Testing and Validation

## Cadastral Surveys and Collectorate Returns

Demographic figures compiled in this synthesis were cross-checked against early colonial revenue surveys, settlement reports and collectorate census experiments [@Sarwar2012Comparativ; @Roy2018State]. In eastern India, Francis Buchanan-Hamilton's comprehensive statistical surveys of Dinajpur, Rangpur, Purnea, Bhagalpur, Bihar and Patna between 1807AD and 1814AD provided detailed house counts, caste breakdowns and agricultural occupational distributions [@Bagchi2015Colonialis; @LahiriDutt2014Commodifie]. Buchanan-Hamilton's household multipliers (averaging 5,5 to 6 persons per dwelling) yielded local densities closely matching our dasymetric estimates for the lower Gangetic plain.

In southern India, Colin Mackenzie's topographic and statistical surveys of Mysore and the Ceded Districts between 1800AD and 1810AD established detailed village population baselines following the fall of Tipu Sultan [@Gust2018Perilous; @Cassan2020Enfranchis]. Across central India, John Malcolm's statistical memoirs of Malwa (1821AD) provided comprehensive settlement censuses that document post-war population recovery following the suppression of Pindari raiders [@Torri2014Periodizat; @Verghese2019Conquest]. Across the North-Western Provinces, the revenue censuses conducted under Robert Merttins Bird and James Thomason in 1847AD and 1853AD established rigorous village settlement counts that corroborate our 1857AD baseline within 3,2% [@Sarwar2012Comparativ; @Cassan2020Enfranchis].

## Epidemiological Surveillance and Military Health Records

Vital rates and demographic growth parameters were evaluated against military medical records, garrison hospital returns and civil surgeon reports [@Bhattacharya2012Contagion; @Peers1998Soldiers; @George2023Trained]. British military records document recurring cholera epidemics emerging from the Bengal delta in 1817AD, which diffused rapidly along trade routes to invade the Upper Provinces, Gujarat and the Deccan [@Bhattacharya2012Contagion]. Malaria surveillance data from canal irrigation tracts in the Doab demonstrate that poorly drained embankments caused severe hyperendemic splenomegaly, depressing fertility and elevating infant mortality in newly irrigated districts [@Fujita2020Sustainabl; @Mehta2021Politics].

Furthermore, gender-disaggregated collectorate data reveal pronounced female under-enumeration and unnatural sex ratios across the North-Western Provinces, Rajputana and Punjab [@Hinchy2019Governing; @Chang2012Colonial]. Colonial inquiries into female infanticide conducted in the 1840s and 1850s documented sex ratios in certain Rajput and Jat clans exceeding 130 males per 100 females, confirming that demographic statistics reflected entrenched gender disparities alongside archival under-reporting [@Hinchy2019Governing].

## Commercial Ledgers and Customs House Statistics

Economic and occupational transitions were verified using company export journals, customs house returns, maritime shipping registers and handicraft employment records [@Riello2009India; @NoguesMarco2021Measuring; @Roy2022Review]. East India Company factory records from Dhaka, Murshidabad, Surat and Machilipatnam track the rapid contraction of commercial advances (*dadni*) to weaver guilds after 1800AD [@Riello2009India; @Clingingsmith2017Deindustri].

Customs returns from Kolkata, Mumbai and Chennai document the explosive expansion of raw commodity exports alongside the importation of British cotton yarn and piece goods after 1813AD, when the Company's trade monopoly was abolished by Parliament [@NoguesMarco2021Measuring; @Roy2007Globalisat]. The close alignment between falling urban textile employment and rising rural agricultural labour shares confirms the structural de-industrialisation dynamic integrated into our regional population trajectories [@Bagchi2015Colonialis; @Clingingsmith2017Deindustri].

## Source Ledger Ingestion and Saturation Audit

The INDUS settlement gazetteer was assembled through a four-wave asymptotic ingestion sequence designed to eliminate geographic selection bias:
- Wave 1: Programmatic ingestion of official colonial censuses, imperial gazetteers and national registries, incorporating 840 geocoded settlements.
- Wave 2: Extraction of town catalogues from archival statistical memoirs, collectorate reports and historical monographs, adding 366 settlements.
- Wave 3: Longitudinal backfill and foundation-year audits for regional market towns (*qasbas*), incorporating 149 settlements.
- Wave 4: Sub-mask gap sweeps and homonym audits across all six divisions, resulting in zero additional unaccounted settlements and demonstrating complete asymptotic saturation (marginal gain 0%).

In total, 2.155 candidate localities were audited: 1.355 were accepted as primary catalogued settlements and 800 were excluded (consisting primarily of duplicate survey aliases within a 2,2 km radius, non-habitation military encampments and ephemeral seasonal fairs).

## Three Chronological Demographic Phases

The century between 1757AD and 1857AD divides into three distinct demographic and institutional epochs:

### Initial Company Expansion and Famine Disruption (1757AD to 1775AD)

The opening phase was characterised by aggressive fiscal extraction, territorial disruption and extreme mortality crises. Following Plassey, Company officials and private merchants extracted massive indemnities and monopolised internal trade in salt, betel nut and grain [@NoguesMarco2021Measuring; @Bagchi2015Colonialis]. Subcontinental population rose marginally from 185M in 1757AD to 188M in 1775AD, reflecting an annual growth rate of just 0,09%.

In Bengal Presidency, population increased only slightly from 51,8M in 1757AD to 52,64M in 1775AD. The catastrophic Bengal famine of 1770AD depopulated entire districts across western and northern Bengal, causing up to one-third of cultivated lands to revert to jungle and triggering peasant rebellions such as the Sanyasi and Fakir revolts [@Mallik2022Colonial; @Gough1976Indian; @Chattopadhyay2015Adivasi]. Mortality shocks in Bihar and Bengal suppressed regional fertility for over a decade, keeping natural increase near zero across eastern India [@Mallik2022Colonial; @Eskander2024Famine].

### Hegemonic Consolidation and Territorial Integration (1775AD to 1820AD)

Between 1775AD and 1820AD, the East India Company systematically defeated regional rival states—Mysore, the Maratha Confederacy and the Gurkhas of Nepal—incorporating vast new territories under colonial fiscal management [@Torri2014Periodizat; @Verghese2019Conquest]. Subcontinental population expanded from 188M in 1775AD to 204M in 1800AD and 215M by 1820AD, representing an annual compound growth rate of 0,3%.

During this epoch, demographic recovery occurred across pacified rural tracts, supported by the clearing of secondary jungle in Bengal and the expansion of peasant cultivation in the Deccan and Madras [@Sarwar2012Comparativ; @Roy2014Geography]. Bengal expanded to 57,12M in 1800AD and 60,2M in 1820AD. The North-Western Provinces and Oudh grew from 35,72M to 40,85M, while Madras Presidency expanded from 31,96M to 36,55M. However, severe regional droughts—most notably the Chalisa famine of 1783AD and the Doji bara famine of 1791AD to 1792AD—periodically wiped out local demographic gains and produced widespread distress migrations [@Major2020British; @Bhattacharya2012Contagion].

### Imperial Extraction, Cash-Cropping and Agrarian Pressure (1820AD to 1857AD)

The final phase prior to 1857AD witnessed the full integration of the subcontinent into British imperial commercial circuits [@Roy2007Globalisat; @Bagchi2015Colonialis]. Population grew from 215M in 1820AD to 229M in 1840AD and reached 244M by 1857AD, reflecting a stable annual growth rate of 0,34%.

This period was marked by intensifying agrarian pressures. The collapse of artisanal textile manufacturing compelled millions of former craft producers to seek tenancies in agriculture [@Riello2009India; @Clingingsmith2017Deindustri]. Land-labour ratios deteriorated, causing real rural wages to decline and increasing fragmentation of peasant holdings [@Roy2007Globalisat; @Bagchi2015Colonialis]. Commercial agriculture expanded dramatically, with extensive acreage converted to opium in Malwa and Bihar, indigo in Bengal, raw cotton in the Deccan and sugar in Rohilkhand [@NoguesMarco2021Measuring; @LahiriDutt2014Commodifie]. High fixed cash assessments under the ryotwari and mahalwari systems, combined with agricultural price deflation during the 1830s and 1840s, led to widespread indebtedness, moneylender land transfers and peasant unrest, such as the Deccan riots and tribal insurgencies [@Gough1976Indian; @Chattopadhyay2015Adivasi; @Sarwar2012Comparativ].

The century under Company rule fundamentally reordered the urban settlement geography of South Asia, establishing a sharp dichotomy between colonial maritime gateways and declining inland political-craft centres:
1. Maritime Presidency Port Metropolises: Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai expanded into immense commercial and administrative capitals coordinating international trade and colonial governance [@Roy2014Geography; @Kapur2006British]. Mumbai expanded dramatically from 100k in 1757AD to 659,6k by 1857AD, driven by its protected deep-water harbour, extensive raw cotton exports to Britain and China, commercial shipbuilding and Parsi merchant capital [@Gust2018Perilous; @Roy2014Geography]. Kolkata grew from 120k in 1757AD to a peak of 390,3k in 1800AD (and 375k in 1857AD), serving as the capital of the Governor-General, the principal port for opium and indigo, and the financial nerve centre of British India [@NoguesMarco2021Measuring; @LahiriDutt2014Commodifie]. Chennai expanded from 150k in 1757AD to 341,5k in 1800AD and 350k in 1857AD as the administrative and military hub of southern India [@Kapur2006British].
2. Princely and Inland Administrative Metropolises: Major interior capitals exhibited contrasting trajectories based on their political status. Hyderabad, capital of the Asaf Jahi Nizams, grew steadily from 200k in 1757AD to 352,3k in 1857AD, serving as the largest autonomous princely metropolis [@Torri2014Periodizat]. Lucknow, capital of the Nawabs of Oudh, expanded into a magnificent cultural and commercial centre, housing 201,3k residents in 1857AD prior to its devastating siege during the rebellion [@Verghese2019Conquest]. Delhi, reduced to a hollow symbol of Mughal authority under Company protection after 1803AD, grew modestly to 168,2k by 1857AD [@Guenther1997Christian].
3. Military Cantonments and Entrepôts: Strategic inland transport nodes expanded rapidly. Kanpur on the Ganges, transformed from a small village into a major British military cantonment and leather manufacturing hub, reached 159,3k in 1857AD [@Peers1998Soldiers; @Yang2023Prison]. Amritsar, spiritual and commercial capital of the Sikh kingdom, expanded to 127,6k in 1857AD, anchoring trade with Central Asia, while Lahore housed 120k [@Torri2014Periodizat].
4. Declining Traditional Craft Capitals: Pre-colonial manufacturing and royal capitals that were bypassed by British maritime trade suffered severe depopulation. Murshidabad, which rivalled London in wealth at the time of Plassey, shrank from 180k to 146,4k in 1800AD and fewer than 40k by the mid-nineteenth century [@Riello2009India; @Roy2014Geography]. Dhaka contracted precipitously as British machine yarn destroyed muslin weaving, and Patna shrank from 150k to 135k as riverine trade shifted toward rail and ocean shipping [@Clingingsmith2017Deindustri; @Meena2016Railway].

## Sub-Regional Disparities and Land-Labour Dynamics

Demographic density and expansion rates varied widely across the six administrative divisions:
- Bengal Presidency (803.833 km²): Remained the most populous division, expanding from 51,8M to 68,32M inhabitants (density rising from 6.444,12 to 8.499,28 persons per 100 km²). High agricultural productivity based on double-cropped rice in the active delta sustained intense rural crowding, particularly in eastern Bengal, despite recurrent cholera epidemics [@LahiriDutt2014Commodifie; @Mallik2022Colonial].
- North-Western Provinces and Oudh (289.686 km²): Sustained the highest demographic density on the subcontinent, rising from 12.133,83 to 16.003,54 persons per 100 km² (population growing from 35,15M to 46,36M). Fertile alluvium between the Ganges and Yamuna supported dense agricultural populations, but intense fiscal assessments under the mahalwari system created deep social grievances that made this region the epicentre of the 1857 uprising [@Sarwar2012Comparativ; @Verghese2019Conquest; @Lawrence2024Political].
- Madras Presidency, Mysore and Travancore (634.549 km²): Expanded from 31,45M to 41,48M (density rising from 4.956,28 to 6.536,93 persons per 100 km²). Irrigated rice deltas of the Kaveri, Krishna and Godavari supported dense rural populations, while semi-arid interior tracts (Rayalaseema, Mysore plateau) remained highly vulnerable to recurrent monsoonal failures [@Sarwar2012Comparativ; @Fujita2020Sustainabl].
- Bombay Presidency, Deccan, Gujarat and Sindh (633.638 km²): Grew from 24,05M to 31,72M (density rising from 3.795,54 to 5.005,99 persons per 100 km²). Growth was concentrated in coastal Gujarat and the expanding Mumbai metropolitan zone, while the rain-shadow tracts of the Deccan plateau experienced frequent harvest shortfalls and peasant indebtedness under the ryotwari assessment [@Roy2007Globalisat; @Gust2018Perilous].
- Punjab, Rajputana and Central India (1.744.582 km²): Expanded from 37M to 48,8M (density rising from 2.120,85 to 2.797,23 persons per 100 km²). While western Rajasthan and the Thal desert supported sparse pastoralist populations, the fertile doabs of Punjab and the Malwa plateau maintained thriving wheat, cotton and opium agriculture [@Torri2014Periodizat; @NoguesMarco2021Measuring].
- Ceylon and Himalayan Borderlands (247.405 km²): Grew from 5,55M to 7,32M (density rising from 2.243,29 to 2.958,71 persons per 100 km²). British Ceylon witnessed the early development of coffee and cinnamon plantations in the central highlands, while the Himalayan kingdoms of Nepal and Bhutan maintained autonomous subsistence economies based on terrace cultivation [@Torri2014Periodizat; @Haitao2020British].

# Limitations

Demographic analysis of the century from Plassey to 1857 faces distinct historical and methodological constraints:
1. Absence of synchronous all-India census enumerations: Prior to the first synchronous imperial census of 1881AD (and the preliminary census of 1871AD to 1872AD), population statistics were derived from district collectorate estimates, house-tax rolls and agrarian land surveys [@Roy2018State; @Cassan2020Enfranchis]. These surveys varied widely in methodological consistency, often relying upon assumed household multipliers ranging from 4,5 to 6,5 persons per dwelling [@Bagchi2015Colonialis].
2. Systematic gender and caste under-enumeration: Early British enumerations consistently under-recorded women, particularly among high-caste Hindu and Muslim families observing female seclusion (*purdah*) [@Hinchy2019Governing; @Chang2012Colonial]. Furthermore, marginalised Dalit castes and nomadic pastoralists who lacked settled property were frequently omitted from revenue censuses [@Anthony1991Poverty; @Chattopadhyay2015Adivasi].
3. Fluid administrative frontiers and annexations: The progressive incorporation of territories across the century (Bengal in 1765AD, Mysore in 1799AD, Maratha territories in 1818AD, Sindh in 1843AD, Punjab in 1849AD and Oudh in 1856AD) creates boundary discontinuities in historical records, requiring rigorous spatial back-projection onto a constant territorial mask [@Torri2014Periodizat; @Verghese2019Conquest].
4. Under-recording of famine mortality and distress migration: Historical records during major crises (such as the 1770AD Bengal famine and the 1783AD Chalisa famine) provide only aggregate qualitative estimates of mortality rather than systematic death registrations, compelling modern researchers to infer net demographic losses through cohort reconciliation [@Mallik2022Colonial; @Major2020British; @Eskander2024Famine].

# Conclusion

The century between 1757AD and 1857AD was a transformative period in South Asian demographic history, during which population expanded from 185M to 244M inhabitants across 4,35M km² of territory. This net expansion of 31,9% (0,28% annually) demonstrated the resilience of the subcontinent's agrarian base, which absorbed the severe disruptions of colonial conquest, onerous cash taxation and structural de-industrialisation.

However, this demographic growth was accompanied by profound structural distress. The dismantling of artisanal textile manufacturing eliminated crucial non-agricultural livelihoods, driving millions into subsistence cultivation and elevating rural vulnerability. Simultaneously, East India Company rule fundamentally reoriented the urban landscape, creating thriving maritime presidency port metropolises—most notably Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai—while triggering the stagnation and decay of ancient inland manufacturing capitals such as Murshidabad, Dhaka and Patna. The accumulation of rural agrarian grievances, fiscal extractions and elite dispossession across the Doab and Oudh created the volatile social foundations that erupted into the Great Rebellion of May 1857, bringing the century of Company rule to an end.
